title: Biology
summary: Life as chemistry that copies itself. Evolution by natural selection is the threshold that organises everything else; the central dogma and homeostasis are the two mechanisms every later topic leans on.
sources: Alberts et al.: Molecular Biology of the Cell
Dobzhansky: Nothing in Biology Makes Sense Except in the Light of Evolution (1973)
Bishop & Anderson: Student conceptions of natural selection (1990)

nodes.label: The Cell
nodes.summary: Membranes, organelles, and the prokaryote–eukaryote divide.
nodes.outcome: Relate an organelle's structure to its function.
nodes.check: What do mitochondria and chloroplasts have that hints at their bacterial origin?
nodes.answer: Their own circular DNA and ribosomes, and double membranes (endosymbiosis).

nodes.label: Biological Macromolecules
nodes.summary: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids, built from monomers by condensation.
nodes.outcome: Identify monomers and bonds for each class.
nodes.check: What bond joins amino acids in a protein?

nodes.label: DNA & the Central Dogma
nodes.summary: DNA is copied (replication), transcribed into RNA, and translated into protein.
nodes.outcome: Transcribe and translate a short sequence.
nodes.check: The DNA template strand reads 3′-TAC-5′. What is the mRNA codon, and which amino acid does it code for?

nodes.label: Protein Structure & Function
nodes.summary: Sequence folds into shape, and shape does the work: primary to quaternary structure.
nodes.outcome: Explain how one amino-acid change can disable a protein.
nodes.check: How does a single amino-acid substitution cause sickle-cell disease?
nodes.answer: Glutamate → valine in haemoglobin makes the proteins stick together and deform red cells.

nodes.label: Enzymes
nodes.summary: Biological catalysts lowering activation energy; saturation kinetics (Michaelis–Menten) and inhibition.
nodes.outcome: Interpret a Michaelis–Menten plot with and without an inhibitor.
nodes.check: Why does an enzyme's rate level off at high substrate concentration?
nodes.answer: All active sites are occupied (saturation), so rate reaches Vmax.

nodes.label: Respiration & Photosynthesis
nodes.summary: Energy flow through redox: glucose to ATP via glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain; light to sugar in chloroplasts.
nodes.outcome: Trace where the ATP from one glucose comes from.
nodes.check: Which stage of aerobic respiration makes most of the ATP?
nodes.answer: Oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport chain and ATP synthase).

nodes.label: Mendelian Genetics
nodes.summary: Alleles segregate and assort; Punnett squares predict offspring ratios.
nodes.check: Two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa) mate. What fraction of offspring show the recessive trait?

nodes.label: "Dominant alleles are more common"
nodes.summary: Dominance describes expression in heterozygotes, not frequency. Huntington's allele is dominant and rare.
nodes.check: Will a dominant allele spread through a population because it is dominant?
nodes.answer: No: frequency changes through selection, drift and migration, not dominance.

nodes.label: Evolution by Natural Selection
nodes.summary: Variation, inheritance and differential reproduction, repeated over generations. Once grasped, it explains why every other biological fact is the way it is.
nodes.outcome: Explain antibiotic resistance with variation and selection.
nodes.check: How do bacterial populations become antibiotic-resistant?
nodes.answer: Resistant variants already present survive and reproduce more, so their frequency rises; individuals do not 'adapt'.

nodes.label: "Organisms evolve because they need to"
nodes.summary: Need does not create variation (the Lamarckian intuition). Selection acts on variation that already exists.
nodes.outcome: Rewrite a teleological explanation in selection terms.
nodes.check: 'Giraffes grew long necks to reach high leaves.' What is wrong, and how should it be rephrased?
nodes.answer: Need does not cause change; giraffes with longer necks left more offspring, so the trait became common.

nodes.label: Population Genetics
nodes.summary: Hardy–Weinberg as the null model; drift, selection, mutation and migration as forces that move allele frequencies.
nodes.outcome: Use Hardy–Weinberg to estimate carrier frequency.
nodes.check: A recessive disease affects 1 in 10,000. Roughly what fraction are carriers?

nodes.label: Gene Regulation
nodes.summary: Which genes are on, when and where: promoters, transcription factors, operons and epigenetics.
nodes.outcome: Explain the lac operon's response to lactose and glucose.
nodes.check: Every cell in your body has the same DNA. Why are neurons different from liver cells?
nodes.answer: Different genes are expressed, controlled by transcription factors and epigenetic marks.

nodes.label: Cell Signalling
nodes.summary: Receptors, second messengers and amplification cascades.
nodes.outcome: Trace a signal from receptor to response.
nodes.check: How can a few hormone molecules cause a large cellular response?
nodes.answer: Signal cascades amplify the signal at each enzymatic step.

nodes.label: Neurons & Action Potentials
nodes.summary: Ion gradients, voltage-gated channels and all-or-nothing spikes; synapses as chemical signals.
nodes.outcome: Explain the phases of an action potential with ion movements.
nodes.check: What causes the rising phase of an action potential?
nodes.answer: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in.

nodes.label: Homeostasis & Feedback
nodes.summary: Negative feedback keeps internal conditions near set points: temperature, glucose, pH.
nodes.outcome: Diagram a negative-feedback loop for blood glucose.
nodes.check: Blood glucose rises after a meal. What hormone responds and what does it do?
nodes.answer: Insulin, which drives cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it, lowering blood glucose.

nodes.label: The Immune System
nodes.summary: Innate and adaptive defences; antibodies, T cells and immunological memory.
nodes.outcome: Explain how a vaccine creates memory.
nodes.check: Why is the second exposure to a pathogen usually milder?
nodes.answer: Memory B and T cells respond faster and more strongly.

nodes.label: Ecology & Energy Flow
nodes.summary: Populations, communities and ecosystems; energy flows one way through trophic levels while matter cycles.
nodes.outcome: Compute energy available at a higher trophic level.
nodes.check: Roughly what fraction of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?

nodes.label: "Energy is recycled in ecosystems"
nodes.summary: Matter cycles; energy flows through and leaves as heat. Ecosystems need a constant energy input (usually sunlight).
nodes.outcome: Distinguish matter cycling from energy flow.
nodes.check: When a decomposer breaks down a dead tree, is the tree's energy returned to plants?
nodes.answer: No: the nutrients cycle, but the energy is lost as heat.

nodes.label: Biotechnology: PCR & CRISPR
nodes.summary: Copying DNA exponentially (PCR) and editing it at chosen sites (CRISPR–Cas9).
nodes.outcome: Explain the steps of PCR and how Cas9 finds its target.
nodes.check: After 30 PCR cycles, roughly how many copies come from one template?
